test_p::optimized.intuition: The optimised solution to "Two Sum" avoids redundant comparisons by exploiting structure in the problem — using a hash map, two pointers, or prefix sums to reduce the inner loop to an O(1) lookup.
test_p::optimized.key_insight: Trade space for time: store seen values so each lookup is O(1).

steps.label: Step 2 — Preprocess (if needed)
steps.detail: Sort or build the auxiliary structure once — O(n) or O(n log n) — paid once.

test_two_sum::optimized.intuition: For each number, calculate the value needed to reach the target. Use a hash map to remember previously seen numbers and their indices, so the needed value can be found in constant average time.
test_two_sum::optimized.key_insight: Instead of checking every pair, look up target minus the current number among values already scanned.

steps.label: Step 1 — initialize the lookup map
steps.detail: Create an empty hash map that will store each previously seen number and its index. The number is the key, and its index is the value.

steps.label: Step 2 — scan the array once
steps.detail: Move from left to right through {INPUT}, examining one number and its index at a time. For the current number, calculate its complement as target minus the number.

steps.label: Step 3 — check for the complement
steps.detail: Look up the complement in the hash map. If it is already present, its stored index and the current index form the required answer.

steps.label: Step 4 — record the current number
steps.detail: If no complement was found, store the current number and its index in the hash map. Checking before storing prevents the same array element from being used twice.

steps.label: Step 5 — return the matching indices
steps.detail: When a complement is found, immediately return the stored index and current index. A valid Two Sum input guarantees that a solution exists.

test_two_sum::optimized.time_complexity: O(n) — each of the n elements is scanned once, and hash map lookup and insertion take O(1) average time
test_two_sum::optimized.space_complexity: O(n) — in the worst case, the hash map stores all n previously seen numbers

trace_template.description: Start with an empty map while preparing to process {INPUT}.
Select the current value and index while scanning {INPUT} from left to right.
Compute target minus the current value from {INPUT}, then check whether that complement exists in the map.
If no match exists yet, add the current value and its index from {INPUT} to the map.
When the complement from {INPUT} is found, return its stored index together with the current index.

common_mistakes: Returning the numbers instead of their indices.
Inserting the current number before checking its complement, which can incorrectly reuse the same element.
Using a nested loop and missing the intended O(n) hash map solution.

step_01___basics_all_divisors::brute.intuition: Instead of finding divisors of each number one by one, flip the perspective: for every number i from 1 to N, count how many numbers up to N have i as a divisor (those are the multiples of i). Each such multiple contributes i to the grand total, so we add i once per multiple.
step_01___basics_all_divisors::brute.key_insight: Every number i contributes itself to the divisor-sum of every multiple of i, so the total is sum of i × floor(N/i) for all i from 1 to N.

steps.label: Step 1 — Initialize accumulator
steps.detail: Start a running total at 0 that will collect the sum of all divisors across all numbers from 1 to N.

steps.label: Step 2 — Pick each candidate divisor
steps.detail: Loop i from 1 to N. Each i is a potential divisor of some numbers in the range.

steps.label: Step 3 — Walk through multiples of i
steps.detail: Use an inner loop with j starting at 1, and while i*j <= N, the number i*j is a multiple of i, so i is one of its divisors.

steps.label: Step 4 — Add i for each multiple
steps.detail: For every valid multiple found, add i to the total. This accounts for i being a divisor of that multiple.

steps.label: Step 5 — Return the grand total
steps.detail: After all i values are processed, the total holds the sum of divisors of every number from 1 to N.

step_01___basics_all_divisors::brute.time_complexity: O(N log N) — for each i, the inner loop runs floor(N/i) times; summing N/i over i=1..N gives roughly N log N.
step_01___basics_all_divisors::brute.space_complexity: O(1) — only a few integer variables are used regardless of N.

trace_template.description: total = 0, N = {INPUT}
For each i from 1 to {INPUT}, treat i as a candidate divisor
j=1; while i*j <= {INPUT}, the value i*j is a multiple of i
Add i to total for each multiple found
After all i processed, return total

common_mistakes: Confusing this with the per-number divisor approach and trying to find divisors of each number individually, which is less intuitive here.
Using i*j < N instead of i*j <= N, which would miss the number N itself as a multiple.
Adding j instead of i to the total — i is the divisor, j is just the multiplier index.
